query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with a predominantly FCC microstructure, elevated‐temperature exposure in oxidizing (or even mildly reducing) environments induces differential oxidation of the constituent elements. This selectively produces a multi‐layered oxide scale – in which protective inner oxides (e.g. Cr2O3 and Al2O3) coexist with less protective, Ti‐rich (or mixed spinel) outer oxide phases – that tends to form preferentially along high‐energy sites such as grain boundaries and residual defects from rapid solidification. The mismatch in mechanical properties and thermal expansion between these oxide layers and the underlying metal results in internal stresses, leading to scale spallation and intergranular cracking that may trigger catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built, additively manufactured alloy featuring an FCC matrix with fine grains, high defect density, and residual stresses from rapid solidification.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled post-heat treatment to modify the grain structure (e.g. coarsening grain boundaries and reducing defect densities) and compare exposures in atmospheres with controlled oxygen partial pressures (oxidizing vs. mildly reducing).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (approximately 850–1050 °C) under controlled oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres for extended durations (tens to hundreds of hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The oxide scale architecture, particularly the formation, composition, and adhesion of multi-layered oxide films (inner Cr2O3/Al2O3 and outer Ti-rich or spinel phases) preferentially developing along grain boundaries and defect sites.
generation.mechanism: Differences in the intrinsic oxidation kinetics of Cr, Al, Ti, and other alloying elements cause selective elemental oxidation and segregation. The high density of grain boundaries and defects (a legacy of the AM process) accelerates oxide nucleation at these sites. As the oxide scales grow, mismatch in thermal expansion and mechanical stiffness between the protective inner layer and the non-protective outer layer leads to stress accumulation. Eventually, spallation of the non-coherent outer oxides occurs, exposing fresh metal and promoting further rapid oxidation and intergranular cracking, which ultimately precipitates catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: In untreated, as-built samples exposed to the oxidizing temperature range, one should observe the formation of a stratified oxide scale with evidence of spallation and intergranular cracks predominantly along grain boundaries; in contrast, samples with modified (coarser) grain structures or in atmospheres that limit oxygen activity would show slower oxide growth, better adhesion of the inner layers, and reduced degradation.
generation.baseline: The as-built alloy state exhibits an FCC matrix with a fine-scale microstructure and limited initial oxidation at moderate temperatures.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism becomes significant above ~850 °C under oxidizing environments; variations in oxygen partial pressure (or under reducing conditions) are expected to modify oxide composition and growth kinetics, potentially delaying the onset of catastrophic spallation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative rates of oxide growth, the specific phase assemblage (especially the nature and proportion of Ti-rich or spinel phases), and the stress thresholds leading to spallation depend sensitively on the details of the as-built microstructure and processing history; further systematic study is needed to refine these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples – one kept in the as-built state and the other subjected to a post-heat treatment intended to reduce defect density and coarsen the grain structure. Expose both sets to high-temperature conditions (850–1050 °C) under a controlled, oxidizing gas atmosphere. Use in situ and ex situ characterization methods (e.g., SEM/TEM imaging to assess the oxide layer structure and adhesion, XRD to identify oxide phases, and mechanical testing such as high-temperature tensile or creep tests) to track oxide growth, spallation events, and degradation progression.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and layer stratification (via cross-sectional SEM/TEM)
Phase identification of oxide scales (via XRD and EDS)
Grain boundary oxidation and crack formation (via high-resolution microscopy)
Changes in mechanical properties (tensile strength, creep life) before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If post-heat treatment (or variations in oxygen partial pressure) does not appreciably alter the layered oxide structure, its adhesion, or the initiation of intergranular cracks relative to the as-built state, or if catastrophic failure is observed without any correlation to oxide spallation and grain boundary oxidation, then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis would be falsified.
